on_shelf.text: In the Quæstionibus theosophicis Boehme makes particular use of the form of Yes and No for the separator, for this opposition. He says: “The reader must know that in Yes and No all things consist, whether divine, devilish, earthly, or what they may be called. The One as the Yes is pure power and life, and it is the truth of God or God Himself.

on_shelf.label: History of Philosophy, Jacob Boehme
on_shelf.text: However rude and barbarous this may on the one hand be, and however impossible it is to read Boehme continuously, or to take a firm grasp of his thoughts (for all these qualities, spirits and angels make one’s head swim), we must on the other hand recognize that he speaks of everything as it is in its actuality, and that he does this from his heart.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Good morning, Ramesh. The tea is welcome. I trust the household is quiet this morning; I shall take my reading to the step before the sun grows too strong.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: Morning, Shri Hegel. Yes, quiet as a library. I’ll have the breakfast ready by seven, if you don’t mind.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: I shall begin the walk now, Ramesh. Thank you for the tea. I will return before the heat settles.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: All right, sir. The gate is unlocked, so you just walk out. I'll keep the sambar warm.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Mr. Malhotra, you have served the state for three decades. In my lectures, I argue that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But you, who have lived within its apparatus, what did it feel like to witness the Idea move through the machinery of bureaucracy? Was there a moment when the machinery seemed to move of its own accord, independent of the spirit it was meant to serve?

typed_records.speaker: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
typed_records.words: I don't know what a 'spirit' is, but I know the difference between a file and a decision. The machinery doesn't move, it waits. You have to push it, and even then, it usually just creaks.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: You mistake the nature of the thing, sir. A machine is dead; it requires a hand from outside to move it. The state is not a machine, but a living organism, the actuality of the ethical idea. It does not creak because it is pushed; it moves because the spirit within it recognizes its own freedom. Your file is stuck not because the machinery is broken, but because it has not yet found the form that corresponds to its content. It must be allowed to grow into its decision, not forced.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Ramesh, the food is good. Tell me, in this house, what is the name of this white cake, and what is the dark sauce? I wish to learn the words of the land before I learn its history.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: That's idli, sir. The dark one is sambar. You'll get used to the words soon enough.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall endeavor to master the sambar as I have mastered the English. Now, if you will excuse me, I must attend to my writing before the heat forces a pause.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: Yes sir, the sambar is waiting in the kitchen. Take your time with the writing.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will return to the table shortly, but for now, the pen has the priority.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: Yes sir. The pen can wait until the sambar gets cold, but I suppose that is your choice. I will be outside if you need anything.

typed_records.text:
13 October 2026. Delhi, 09:14.

The sun has already pressed the air into a stillness that feels less like weather and more like a metaphysical condition. I sat on the step this morning, reading the papers, noting the tensions between the protest and the administration. It is a spectacle of civil society in its raw, unmediated form. Yet, as I walk through Lodhi Gardens, observing the tombs of the Sayyids and the Lodis, I am reminded of a fundamental distinction that has been occupying my mind these past days in this bungalow on Tughlak Road.

The Hindu burns his dead and leaves no house; these domes are the conquerors' work. A country taken in turn by everyone has a history the way a road has traffic. This is not a history of spirit, but of nature. In the Oriental world, freedom is not yet a substantial idea. It is an individual freedom, a dream. The many gods of India are not the one God who reveals Himself in history, but a pantheon that reflects the undifferentiated, natural state of the mind. The castes are fixed like nature, unchangeable, a hierarchy that is given rather than grown. There is no state of its own making, no ethical substance that has achieved self-consciousness.

Contrast this with the Germanic world, where freedom is the end and the beginning. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is not a contract, a mere mechanism of wills, but the organic unity of the particular and the universal. In the Germanic constitution, the individual finds his freedom not in isolation from the whole, but in his participation in it. The law is not an external constraint, but the expression of the rational will.

India stands at the dawn of that history, outside its movement. It is a spirit that dreams. It has not yet passed through the dialectic of master and slave, of struggle and recognition, to arrive at the ethical life of the state. The many gods are a reflection of this lack of unity. The mind has not yet achieved the self-difference necessary to recognize the other as a free being, and thus to constitute itself as a free being.

I think of my own position here. I am a ghost, a mistake in the allotment of the Directorate. I am Hegel, not Hegde. I am a spirit in a body that does not belong to me, in a land that does not recognize me. Yet, in this very alienation, I find a clarity of vision. I am outside the movement, looking in. I see the dream for what it is, and the state for what it is. The dream is beautiful, but it is not free. The state is rational, and therefore free.

I must return to the table. Ramesh has kept the sambar warm. The body demands its fuel, but the mind must continue its work. The difference between dream and state is not a matter of preference, but of reason. It is the difference between nature and spirit, between the given and the grown. I shall write on this further, but for now, I must eat.
typed_records.title: On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

typed_records.text: Ramesh hands over a note from Shri G. Hegde: he would like to call on Monday at ten, to settle the matter of the bungalow like gentlemen.
Word from Masterji, through Ramesh: the bandhgala is ready. The balance is ₹3,500.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall go to Khan Market now to settle the balance with Masterji. Please keep the sambar warm until my return.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: Yes sir, the sambar is warm, but the balance is due before you leave. Please hand over the three thousand five hundred rupees now.

typed_records.text: Masterji says a dealer in Sunder Nagar would pay ₹12,000 in cash for a genuine Berlin frock coat.
He keeps the coat. Masterji nods: it is a good coat.

typed_records.speaker: Masterji
typed_records.words: You are late, sir. The bandhgala is waiting, and the balance is due. Pay the three thousand five hundred, and we will discuss the coat.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Masterji, the balance is due. Here is the three thousand five hundred rupees. As for the frock coat, I am not a dealer in antiques, nor do I wish to sell my history to a man in Sunder Nagar. I will keep the coat; it is a relic of a world that has passed, but it is still mine. And please, no sambar until the transaction is concluded.

typed_records.speaker: Masterji
typed_records.words: The money is counted. The coat is yours to keep, as you say. I will not argue with a man who values a ghost over cash.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Thank you, Masterji. The fit is acceptable. I shall return when the season turns, or when the spirit requires a new collar.

typed_records.speaker: Masterji
typed_records.words: Season turns or not, the collar is cut tight. If it chokes you, that is your business.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Ramesh, the heat is quite oppressive. I will sit and rest until the meal is ready. Do not bring the sambar now; let it cool further if it must, but ensure the tea is fresh.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: Yes sir, fresh tea it is. I will keep the sambar on the low flame, though it will be better if we eat before it gets too cold.

typed_records.speaker: Hegel
typed_records.words: Very good, Ramesh. I shall take a brief walk to cool the head. Return the sambar when I come back; it shall not be wasted.

typed_records.speaker: Ramesh
typed_records.words: Yes sir. I will wait for you. Just do not take too long, the sambar is delicate.

typed_records.text: Read the papers on the step and note the tensions in the headlines regarding protest and administration.
Walk to Lodhi Gardens to observe the tombs and the morning light on the architecture.
Return home to write in the journal, reflecting on the difference between dream and state.
Prepare a simple meal of bread and tea, as no household food is available.
Sort the pending vouchers and check the cash to ensure the dhobi payment is ready for Saturday.
Take a short evening walk around the bungalow to cool down before the night.
